mathprize-2023-01.title: Set up the side-length equation
mathprize-2023-01.body:
Let $L$ and $S$ be the long and short bases (in inches). The frame is $5''$ wide, so each trapezoid has height $5$, and with $45^\circ$ base angles $L=S+10$.

Along one outer edge there are $n$ long bases and $n-1$ short ones (alternating, starting and ending with long), so
$$nL+(n-1)S=n(2S+10)-S=105,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad S(2n-1)=105-10n.$$
We need $S>0$, so $10n<105$, $n\le10$. With $n=10$, $S=\frac{5}{19}>0$ works. Each side then has $2n-1=19$ trapezoids, for a total of $4\cdot19=76$ (each trapezoid touches exactly one outer edge).

**Answer: 76**

mathprize-2023-01.title: Limiting triangles
mathprize-2023-01.body:
Imagine shrinking the short base to $0$: each trapezoid becomes a right isosceles triangle with hypotenuse $10''$ on the outer edge (height $5''$). At most $\lfloor105/10\rfloor=10$ such hypotenuses fit along a side, with $9$ inverted triangles between them: $19$ pieces per side. Now enlarge all the pieces slightly (short bases $S=\frac5{19}$) until the $10$ long bases plus $9$ short bases fill exactly $105''$. With $11$ long bases we would already need $110''>105''$. So the maximum is $4\cdot19=76$.

**Answer: 76**

mathprize-2023-02.title: Vieta
mathprize-2023-02.body:
The $x$-coordinates $p,q,r$ of $P,Q,R$ are the roots of $2x^3+6x^2-4x+5-k=0$, so $p+q+r=-\frac62=-3$. Since $Q$ is the midpoint, $p+r=2q$, hence $3q=-3$ and $q=-1$.

Then $k$ is the value of the cubic at $x=-1$: $2(-1)^3+6(-1)^2-4(-1)+5=-2+6+4+5=13$.

**Answer: 13**

mathprize-2023-02.title: Point of symmetry
mathprize-2023-02.body:
Every cubic is symmetric about its inflection point. Here $y''=12x+12=0$ at $x=-1$. A horizontal line meeting the cubic in three points with the middle one the midpoint must pass through the center of symmetry (shift so $Q$ is the origin: the cubic becomes $2x(x-r)(x+r)$, which is odd, so $Q$ is the inflection point). So $k=y(-1)=13$.

**Answer: 13**

mathprize-2023-03.title: Complement pairs and a construction
mathprize-2023-03.body:
Let $U$ be the union, with $|U|=u$.

**$u\le12$ is impossible:** a $12$-element set has only $2^{12}=4096<5000$ subsets.

**$u=13$ is impossible:** the $2^{13}=8192$ subsets of $U$ form $4096$ pairs $\{X,U\setminus X\}$. With $5000>4096$ sets, two of our sets form such a pair, and they are disjoint — contradiction.

**$u=14$ works:** the number of subsets of a $14$-set with at least $8$ elements is $\frac{2^{14}-\binom{14}{7}}{2}=\frac{16384-3432}{2}=6476\ge5000$. Take the $14$ subsets of size $13$ and $4986$ other subsets of size between $8$ and $13$ (not the whole set $U$). Any two sets of size $\ge8$ in a $14$-set intersect ($8+8>14$). The intersection of all of them is empty, because no element lies in all $14$ of the $13$-element subsets. The union is $U$ (each element lies in some $13$-subset).

So the minimum is $14$.

**Answer: 14**

mathprize-2023-04.title: The intersection is a regular hexagon
mathprize-2023-04.body:
The six points $B_k$, $C_k$ are the trisection points of the sides. Reflection in any altitude of the big triangle swaps $\triangle B_1B_2B_3$ and $\triangle C_1C_2C_3$, so the intersection has all the symmetries of the equilateral triangle.

Each side of $\triangle B_1B_2B_3$ joins trisection points on two sides: e.g. near vertex $A_1$ it joins the point $\frac13$ from $A_1$ on one side to the point $\frac23$ from $A_1$ on the other side. In a $60^\circ$ angle, the segment from distance $\frac13$ to distance $\frac23$ is perpendicular to the first side (the triangle with sides $\frac13,\frac23$ and included angle $60^\circ$ is a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle). So every side of the intersection is perpendicular to a side of the big triangle: the hexagon's sides point in $6$ directions $60^\circ$ apart, its angles are $120^\circ$, and with the symmetry it is a regular hexagon.

Opposite sides of the hexagon are the perpendiculars at distances $\frac13$ and $\frac23$ along a side, so the distance between them is $\frac13$. A regular hexagon with width $\frac13$ consists of $6$ equilateral triangles of height $\frac16$. The big triangle has height $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, so each small triangle has area ratio $\left(\frac{1/6}{\sqrt3/2}\right)^2=\frac1{27}$, and the hexagon has $\frac{6}{27}=\frac29$ of the area.

**Answer: $\frac{2}{9}$**

mathprize-2023-04.title: Coordinates
mathprize-2023-04.body:
Take $A_1=(0,0)$, $A_2=(1,0)$, $A_3=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$. The perpendiculars to $A_1A_2$ at the trisection points are $x=\frac13$ and $x=\frac23$; these are sides of the two triangles (by the $30$-$60$-$90$ observation). The hexagon is bounded by the three pairs of such lines, so it is the regular hexagon centered at the centroid $\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{6}\right)$ with inradius $\frac16$ (half the distance $\frac13$ between opposite sides).

A regular hexagon with inradius $\rho$ has area $2\sqrt3\rho^2=2\sqrt3\cdot\frac1{36}=\frac{\sqrt3}{18}$. The big triangle has area $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}$. Ratio: $\frac{\sqrt3/18}{\sqrt3/4}=\frac{4}{18}=\frac29$. (A computer polygon intersection confirms $0.2222\ldots$)

**Answer: $\frac{2}{9}$**

mathprize-2023-05.title: Three corner triangles
mathprize-2023-05.body:
Let $H_A,H_B,H_C$ be the feet of the altitudes. Triangle $AH_BH_C$ is similar to $ABC$ with ratio $\cos A$ (since $AH_B=AB\cos A$, $AH_C=AC\cos A$, and the angle at $A$ is shared, with the vertices swapped). Similarly the corner triangles at $B$ and $C$ have ratios $\cos B$ and $\cos C$.

The orthic triangle plus the three corner triangles make up $ABC$, so
$$870-48=870(\cos^2A+\cos^2B+\cos^2C)\ \Rightarrow\ \cos^2A+\cos^2B+\cos^2C=1-\frac{48}{870}.$$
Therefore $\sin^2A+\sin^2B+\sin^2C=3-\left(1-\frac{48}{870}\right)=2+\frac{8}{145}=\frac{298}{145}$.

**Answer: $\frac{298}{145}$**

mathprize-2023-05.title: Known identities
mathprize-2023-05.body:
The orthic triangle of an acute triangle has area $2K\cos A\cos B\cos C$, where $K$ is the area of $ABC$. So $\cos A\cos B\cos C=\frac{48}{2\cdot870}=\frac{4}{145}$.

In any triangle $\cos^2A+\cos^2B+\cos^2C+2\cos A\cos B\cos C=1$, so
$$\sin^2A+\sin^2B+\sin^2C=3-(\cos^2A+\cos^2B+\cos^2C)=2+2\cos A\cos B\cos C=2+\frac{8}{145}=\frac{298}{145}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{298}{145}$**

mathprize-2023-06.title: Interpolating polynomial
mathprize-2023-06.body:
Let $p(a)=v+wa+xa^2+ya^3+za^4$. The equations say $p(-1)=79$, $p(1)=-1$, $p(2)=-2$, $p(3)=-1$, $p(5)=79$.

These values fit $q(a)=(a-2)^4-2$: $q(-1)=81-2$, $q(1)=1-2$, $q(2)=-2$, $q(3)=1-2$, $q(5)=81-2$. ✓ A polynomial of degree at most $4$ is determined by $5$ values, so $p=q$, and $x$ is the coefficient of $a^2$ in $(a-2)^4-2$:
$$x=\binom42(-2)^2=24.$$

**Answer: 24**

mathprize-2023-06.title: Lagrange / finite differences check
mathprize-2023-06.body:
Directly solving the $5\times5$ linear system (e.g. by elimination) gives $(v,w,x,y,z)=(14,-32,24,-8,1)$: indeed $(a-2)^4-2=a^4-8a^3+24a^2-32a+14$. Checking the third equation: $14-64+96-64+16=-2$. ✓

**Answer: 24**

mathprize-2023-07.title: Only runs of length 1 and 3
mathprize-2023-07.body:
The expression is a sum of powers $(\sqrt3)^m$, one for each maximal run of $m$ multiplied $\sqrt3$'s, and $m_1+m_2+\dots=12$. The value has the form $a+b\sqrt3$ with $a$ coming from even powers; since we need $a=0$, every run has odd length.

Compare each run with its "fair share" $m\sqrt3$: $(\sqrt3)^1=1\cdot\sqrt3$, $(\sqrt3)^3=3\sqrt3$, but $(\sqrt3)^{2k+1}=3^k\sqrt3>(2k+1)\sqrt3$ for $k\ge2$. The total is $12\sqrt3=\sum m_i\sqrt3$ exactly, so every run must have length $1$ or $3$.

Count compositions of $12$ into parts $1$ and $3$: with $j$ threes there are $12-3j$ ones and $\binom{12-2j}{j}$ arrangements:
$j=0$: $1$; $j=1$: $\binom{10}{1}=10$; $j=2$: $\binom82=28$; $j=3$: $\binom63=20$; $j=4$: $\binom44=1$. Total $60$.

Probability $\frac{60}{2^{11}}=\frac{15}{512}$.

**Answer: $\frac{15}{512}$**

mathprize-2023-07.title: Recursion
mathprize-2023-07.body:
Let $c_n$ be the number of ways to write $n$ as an ordered sum of $1$'s and $3$'s (equivalently, tile a $1\times n$ strip with $1\times1$ and $1\times3$ tiles). Then $c_n=c_{n-1}+c_{n-3}$ with $c_0=c_1=c_2=1$:
$$1,1,1,2,3,4,6,9,13,19,28,41,60,$$
so $c_{12}=60$ sign patterns work (as argued, the runs must have length $1$ or $3$), and the probability is $\frac{60}{2048}=\frac{15}{512}$. A computer check of all $2048$ patterns agrees.

**Answer: $\frac{15}{512}$**

mathprize-2023-08.title: Case on $p(n)$
mathprize-2023-08.body:
The inequality says $n\le4^{p(n)}$.

- If $p(n)\ge5$: $n\ge2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=2310>4^5=1024$, and each further prime factor is $>4$, multiplying $n$ by more than the bound grows. No solutions.
- $p(n)=0$: $n=1$ works ($\log_41=0$).
- $p(n)=1$: $n\le4$ and a prime power: $2,3,4$.
- $p(n)=2$: $n\le16$ with exactly two primes: $6,10,12,14,15$.
- $p(n)=3$: $n\le64$ with three primes: $30,42,60$.
- $p(n)=4$: $n\le256$ with four primes: only $210$ (the next, $330$, is too big).

Total $1+3+5+3+1=13$.

**Answer: 13**

mathprize-2023-08.title: Brute force
mathprize-2023-08.body:
Since $p(n)\le4$ for all solutions (shown above), all solutions satisfy $n\le256$. Checking every $n\le256$ (or by computer up to $10^5$) gives exactly the $13$ solutions
$$1,2,3,4,6,10,12,14,15,30,42,60,210.$$

**Answer: 13**

mathprize-2023-09.title: Count by spokes
mathprize-2023-09.body:
Call the $6$ hexagons touching the center the *inner layer* and the other $12$ the *outer layer*. A *spoke* is a tile covering an inner hexagon and the outer hexagon directly outward from it (across the edge on the radial line through the center). Two spokes cannot be adjacent (that would isolate a hexagon), so there are $0$, $1$, $2$ or $3$ spokes.

- **0 spokes:** the inner layer (a $6$-cycle) and the outer layer (a $12$-cycle) are tiled separately, each in $2$ ways: $4$.
- **1 spoke:** for a fixed spoke, consider the hexagon that touches both spoke hexagons; the tile covering it can go two ways, leading to $1$ and $5$ completions respectively: $6$ per spoke, $6\cdot6=36$.
- **2 spokes:** opposite spokes split the rest into two parts of $7$ hexagons (odd — impossible). So they are $120^\circ$ apart, splitting the rest into parts of $4$ and $10$ hexagons, tiled in $2$ and $4$ ways: $8$ per placement, $6$ placements: $48$.
- **3 spokes:** evenly spaced ($2$ placements), leaving three $4$-hexagon parts with $2$ tilings each: $2\cdot8=16$.

Total $4+36+48+16=104$.

**Answer: 104**

mathprize-2023-09.title: Computer enumeration
mathprize-2023-09.body:
Label hexagons by axial coordinates $(q,r)$; the ring consists of the $18$ cells at hex-distance $1$ or $2$ from the center. Two cells are adjacent if they differ by one of $(\pm1,0),(0,\pm1),(1,-1),(-1,1)$. A tiling is a perfect matching of this adjacency graph. Recursively choosing the partner of the first uncovered cell counts the perfect matchings: $104$.

**Answer: 104**

mathprize-2023-10.title: Use $4096=2^{12}$
mathprize-2023-10.body:
Note $4099-3=4096=2^{12}$, so $-3\equiv 2^{12}=(2^4)^3=16^3\pmod{4099}$: $16$ is a cube root of $-3$. Hence the cube roots of $3$ are $-16\omega$ where $\omega$ runs over the cube roots of $1$. Since $3\mid4098$, there are three: $1$ and $\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{-3}}{2}$.

$\sqrt{-3}\equiv\sqrt{2^{12}}=2^6=64$. So $\omega\in\left\{1,\ \frac{63}{2},\ \frac{-65}{2}\right\}$ and
$$x\equiv-16,\quad -16\cdot\tfrac{63}{2}=-504,\quad -16\cdot\left(-\tfrac{65}{2}\right)=520.$$
Reducing mod $4099$: $4083$, $3595$, $520$.

A cubic has at most $3$ roots modulo a prime, so these are all the solutions.

**Answer: $520,\ 3595,\ 4083$**

mathprize-2023-10.title: Search check
mathprize-2023-10.body:
Testing all $x$ from $0$ to $4098$ for $x^3\equiv3\pmod{4099}$ (e.g. with a short program) gives exactly $520$, $3595$, $4083$. Their sum is $8198=2\cdot4099\equiv0$, consistent with Vieta for $x^3-3$ (no $x^2$ term).

**Answer: $520,\ 3595,\ 4083$**

mathprize-2023-11.title: Cases on the angle
mathprize-2023-11.body:
The angle is $15(t-1)^\circ\in\{15^\circ,30^\circ,\dots,165^\circ\}$.

- $t=7$: the angle is $90^\circ$, always right. Probability $\frac{6}{36}=\frac16$.
- $t>7$: the angle is obtuse — never right.
- $t<7$: the right angle is opposite $a$ or $b$, so $a\cos\theta=b$ or $b\cos\theta=a$ — $\cos\theta$ must be rational. Among $15^\circ,30^\circ,45^\circ,60^\circ,75^\circ$ only $\cos60^\circ=\frac12$ is rational ($t=5$, probability $\frac4{36}$), and then $a=2b$ or $b=2a$.

$P(a=2b)$: $(a,b)=(4,2),(6,3),(8,4),(10,5),(12,6)$ with weights $3\cdot1+5\cdot2+5\cdot3+3\cdot4+1\cdot5=45$, so $\frac{45}{36^2}$. Same for $b=2a$, and these are exclusive.

Total: $\frac16+\frac{4}{36}\cdot\frac{2\cdot45}{1296}=\frac16+\frac{360}{46656}=\frac16+\frac{5}{648}=\frac{113}{648}$.

**Answer: $\frac{113}{648}$**

mathprize-2023-11.title: Brute-force check
mathprize-2023-11.body:
Loop over all $11^3$ triples $(a,b,t)$ with dice-sum weights, compute the third side by the law of cosines, and test the Pythagorean relation. The total weight of right triangles divided by $36^3$ is $\frac{113}{648}$, agreeing with the case analysis.

**Answer: $\frac{113}{648}$**

mathprize-2023-12.title: Reduce to coprime pairs
mathprize-2023-12.body:
Write $d=\gcd(A,B)$, $A=ad$, $B=bd$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1$. Then $\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(A,B)}{A+B}=\frac{abd}{(a+b)d}=\frac{ab}{a+b}$. So $S=\left\{\frac{ab}{a+b}:\gcd(a,b)=1\right\}$. Take $a<b$ ($a=b$ forces $a=b=1$, value $\frac12$).

Write $\frac{ab}{a+b}=a-\frac{a^2}{a+b}$, increasing in $b$ and less than $a$. Its smallest value (at $b=a+1$) is $\frac{a(a+1)}{2a+1}>\frac a2$. So for $a\le3$ all values are $<3$, and for $a\ge7$ all values are $>\frac72$. Check $a=4,5,6$:

- $a=4$: $\frac{4b}{4+b}>3\iff b>12$; $b=13$ gives $\frac{52}{17}\approx3.059$.
- $a=5$: $\frac{5b}{5+b}>3\iff b>7.5$; $b=8$ gives $\frac{40}{13}\approx3.077$.
- $a=6$: $\frac{6b}{6+b}>3\iff b>6$; $b=7$ gives $\frac{42}{13}\approx3.23$.

The smallest is $\frac{52}{17}$.

**Answer: $\frac{52}{17}$**

mathprize-2023-12.title: Distance above 3
mathprize-2023-12.body:
$\frac{ab}{a+b}-3=\frac{ab-3a-3b}{a+b}=\frac{(a-3)(b-3)-9}{a+b}$. The numerator is a positive integer, so the difference is at least $\frac1{a+b}$; we want a small positive numerator with a large $a+b$. Numerator $1$: $(a-3)(b-3)=10$ gives $(a,b)=(4,13)$ or $(5,8)$ (coprime), with differences $\frac1{17}$ and $\frac1{13}$. Numerator $k\ge2$ needs $\frac{k}{a+b}<\frac1{17}$, i.e. $a+b>17k$, while $(a-3)(b-3)=9+k$ forces $a+b\le (9+k)+7=k+16$ (when $a=4$) — too small. So the minimum is $3+\frac1{17}=\frac{52}{17}$, attained at $A=4$, $B=13$.

**Answer: $\frac{52}{17}$**

mathprize-2023-13.title: Möbius maps send the real line to a circle
mathprize-2023-13.body:
$f$ is a Möbius transformation, so it maps the real line to a circle (or line). Compute $P=f(0)=\frac{-10+9i}{i}=9+10i$, $R=f(1)=\frac{(10+9i)-10+9i}{1+i}=\frac{18i}{1+i}=9+9i$, and $S=\lim_{t\to\infty}f(t)=10+9i$.

$P=(9,10)$, $R=(9,9)$, $S=(10,9)$ are three vertices of a unit square with $PR$ a side and $PS$ a diagonal. The image of the real line is the circle through them: the circumcircle of the square, centered at $\left(\frac{19}{2},\frac{19}{2}\right)$ with radius $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$. $Q=f(2023)$ is on this circle, and since $t=2023$ is between $1$ and $\infty$ on the real line, $Q$ lies on the arc from $R$ to $S$ not containing $P$. The inscribed angle $\angle PQR$ subtends the chord $PR$, a side of the inscribed square, whose arc is $90^\circ$; so $\angle PQR=45^\circ$ and $\sin^2=\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

mathprize-2023-13.title: Numerical check
mathprize-2023-13.body:
Computing directly, $Q=f(2023)\approx 10.0000+9.0005i$ (very close to $S$). The angle between $\vec{QP}$ and $\vec{QR}$ evaluates to $45^\circ$ to many decimal places, giving $\sin^2\angle PQR=\frac12$. In fact $|f(t)-(\tfrac{19}{2}+\tfrac{19}{2}i)|=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$ for every real $t$, so every $f(t)$ with $t>1$ gives the same inscribed angle.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

mathprize-2023-14.title: The hull is a triangular bipyramid
mathprize-2023-14.body:
With probability $1$ no four points are coplanar, and all five points are vertices of their convex hull (they lie on a sphere). All faces are triangles, so $2E=3F$, and Euler's formula $5-E+F=2$ gives $F=6$, $E=9$. The degree sum is $18$, so some vertex $A$ has degree $4$; the $4$ faces at $A$ and the remaining $2$ faces show the hull is a **triangular bipyramid**: two apexes $U,W$ (degree $3$, not joined) over a triangle $XYZ$ (degree $4$ each).

For a pair of points, the "other three" span a plane; the pair is on the same side iff that triangle is a face of the hull (a face plane has all other points on one side; a non-face triangle of a convex polytope in general position separates the other two).

The $10$ pairs and their complementary triples:
- $\{U,X\}$ etc. (an apex and an equator vertex, $6$ pairs): the complement, e.g. $\{W,Y,Z\}$, is a face — not separated.
- $\{X,Y\}$ etc. ($3$ pairs): complement $\{U,W,Z\}$ is not a face ($U,W$ aren't adjacent) — separated.
- $\{U,W\}$: complement $\{X,Y,Z\}$, not a face — separated.

So $4$ of $10$ pairs work: probability $\frac25$.

**Answer: $\frac25$**

mathprize-2023-14.title: Monte Carlo check
mathprize-2023-14.body:
Simulating $200{,}000$ trials (random points from normalized Gaussian vectors, random pair, sign test against the plane of the other three) gives a frequency of about $0.401$, consistent with $\frac25$.

**Answer: $\frac25$**

mathprize-2023-15.title: Classify the tilings
mathprize-2023-15.body:
Two triangles glued together form a triangle, a quadrilateral (if glued edge-to-edge), or a non-convex pentagon/hexagon. In particular a convex quadrilateral is split into two triangles only by a diagonal. Let the square be $ABCD$.

**Case 1: some corner of the square is a full angle of a tile.** That angle ($90^\circ$) must be the apex of an isosceles right triangle $AXY$ with $X\in AB$, $Y\in AD$. A case check shows we may take $X=B$, $Y=D$ (otherwise the remaining pentagon cannot be cut into three isosceles triangles). Then triangle $BCD$ must be cut into three isosceles triangles. One tile contains side $BC$ with third vertex $Z$ on $BD$, and $Z$ is either the center of the square or the point of $BD$ with $BZ=BC$:
- $Z$ = center: $CDZ$ is a right isosceles triangle, split into two right isosceles triangles. Angles: $45^\circ,90^\circ$.
- $BZ=BC$: triangle $BCZ$ has angles $45^\circ,67.5^\circ,67.5^\circ$; $CDZ$ has angles $45^\circ,22.5^\circ,112.5^\circ$ and splits only into a right isosceles triangle and a $22.5^\circ$-$22.5^\circ$-$135^\circ$ triangle. Angles: $22.5,45,67.5,90,135$.

**Case 2: every corner is split.** Then each side of the square belongs to its own tile, and these four tiles $ABX$, $BCY$, $CDZ$, $DAW$ fill the square; one shows $X=Y=Z=W$ is an interior point joined to the four corners. Either it is the center (four right isosceles triangles: $45^\circ,90^\circ$), or by the isosceles conditions $ABX$ is equilateral and $X$ is the apex: triangles with angles $60^\circ$; $30^\circ$-$75^\circ$-$75^\circ$ (twice); and $15^\circ$-$15^\circ$-$150^\circ$.

The distinct angles are $15,22.5,30,45,60,67.5,75,90,135,150$ (degrees), with sum
$$15+22.5+30+45+60+67.5+75+90+135+150=690.$$

**Answer: 690**

mathprize-2023-16.title: Rotate to roots of iterates of $f$
mathprize-2023-16.body:
$x^2+\frac34=-\left((ix)^2-\frac34\right)=-f(ix)$, and $f$ is even, so $f^{(n)}(x^2+\frac34)=f^{(n)}(f(ix))=f^{(n+1)}(ix)$. Hence $R$ is a $90^\circ$ rotation of $S$, the union of the roots of $f^{(m)}$ for $m\ge2$. Both sets are symmetric about both axes.

**Bounding $S$.** If $|z|=s$, then $|f(z)+\frac34|=s^2$, so $|f(z)|\ge s^2-\frac34$, which is $\ge\frac32$ when $s\ge\frac32$. So the orbit of a point with $|z|\ge\frac32$ stays outside the open disk of radius $\frac32$ and never reaches $0$. Thus $S$ lies inside the disk $|z|<\frac32$.

**Horizontal extent of $S$:** $r_n=\sqrt{\frac34+\sqrt{\frac34+\cdots}}$ ($n$ nested roots) is a root of $f^{(n)}$, and $r_n\to\frac32$. So the real parts of $S$ fill out $\left(-\frac32,\frac32\right)$ in the limit: width $3$.

**Vertical extent:** $\sqrt{\frac34-r_n}$, which approaches $i\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, is (up to sign) a root, so the height is at least $\sqrt3$. Conversely, for $z=t+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}i$, $f(z)=(t^2-\frac32)+\sqrt3\,t\,i$ traces a parabola whose points have $|f(z)|=\sqrt{t^4+\frac94}\ge\frac32$; points with larger imaginary part map further out (to the left of this parabola), so they never reach $0$. Hence the imaginary parts of $S$ stay within $\pm\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

So $S$'s bounding box is $3\times\sqrt3$; $R$'s is $\sqrt3\times3$, area $3\sqrt3$, whose square is $27$.

**Answer: 27**

mathprize-2023-16.title: Numerical check
mathprize-2023-16.body:
The roots can be generated exactly by backward iteration: the roots of $f^{(n)}$ come from $0$ by repeatedly applying $w\mapsto\pm\sqrt{w+\frac34}$, and then $x=\pm\sqrt{w-\frac34}$ gives the roots of $f^{(n)}(x^2+\frac34)$. Doing this for $n\le14$, the largest real part is $0.86602\ldots\approx\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and the largest imaginary part is $1.49999\ldots\approx\frac32$, so the bounding box approaches $\sqrt3\times3$ and the square of its area approaches $27$.

**Answer: 27**

mathprize-2023-17.title: Two triangular pyramids
mathprize-2023-17.body:
Put $C=[0,1]^3$ and $D=[\frac12,\frac32]^3$. The line through the centers is the common space diagonal direction $(1,1,1)$. Near the overlap, $C$ is the corner at $(1,1,1)$ (three edges coming out of it in directions $-e_1,-e_2,-e_3$) and $D$ is the corner at $(\frac12,\frac12,\frac12)$ (edges in directions $+e_1,+e_2,+e_3$). Projected onto the plane perpendicular to the axis, these $6$ edges are $6$ spokes $60^\circ$ apart, so a $60^\circ$ rotation of $D$ about the axis brings each edge of $D$ from its corner into alignment with the projection of an edge of $C$ (a $\pm60^\circ$ rotation gives the same result, by the $120^\circ$ symmetry of the cube).

By symmetry, matched edges then meet in the plane bisecting the segment between the centers. That plane is at distance $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}$ from each corner along the axis; an edge from a corner rises $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ along the axis per unit length, so it reaches the plane after length $\frac{\sqrt3/4}{1/\sqrt3}=\frac34<1$ — inside the edge. Hence $C\cap D'$ is two congruent regular triangular pyramids glued along an equilateral triangle in the bisecting plane, with lateral edges $\frac34$ along the cube edges: the base has side $\frac34\sqrt2$ and each pyramid has height $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}$.

Each pyramid is the corner of a cube cut off at distance $\frac34$ along the three edges, with volume $\frac16\left(\frac34\right)^3=\frac{9}{128}$. Twice that is $\frac{9}{64}$.

**Answer: $\frac{9}{64}$**

mathprize-2023-17.title: Monte Carlo check
mathprize-2023-17.body:
Sampling $2$ million random points of $C$ and testing whether the inverse rotation sends them into $D$ gives a fraction $\approx0.1408$, matching $\frac{9}{64}=0.140625$.

**Answer: $\frac{9}{64}$**

mathprize-2023-18.title: Add strands one at a time
mathprize-2023-18.body:
For each integer $k\ge0$, the part of the graph with $\sqrt k\le x\le\sqrt{k+1}$ is a *strand* crossing the unit square from bottom to top (it lies in one lattice square because $x$ hits an integer only where $x^2$ is an integer). Strands in the same column never meet. Adding a strand that crosses the existing picture at $c$ new interior points (counted as distinct points) adds $c+1$ regions.

Two strands, at positions $x+m$ and $x+n$ with $0<x<1$, meet where $(x+m)^2-(x+n)^2=2x(m-n)+m^2-n^2$ is an integer, i.e. $2xd\in\mathbb Z$ with $d=m-n$. So crossing points lie over $x$ with denominator dividing $2d$; new points for exactly $d$ are $x=\frac j{2d}$ in lowest terms with denominator not dividing $2d'$ for smaller $d'$: $L(1)=1$ ($x=\frac12$), $L(2)=2$, $L(3)=4$, $L(4)=4$, $L(5)=8$ (for $d>1$, $L(d)=2\varphi(d)$).

Let $N(n)$ be the count for domain $[0,n]$. The strands for $n\le x\le n+1$ are $(n+1)^2-n^2$ new strands, and in total they cross the earlier picture at $\sum_{d=1}^{n}L(d)$ distinct points. Hence $N(n+1)=N(n)+(n+1)^2-n^2+\sum_{d\le n}L(d)$, with $N(1)=2$:
$$N(2)=2+3+1=6,\ N(3)=6+5+3=14,\ N(4)=14+7+7=28,\ N(5)=28+9+11=48,\ N(6)=48+11+19=78.$$

**Answer: 78**

mathprize-2023-18.title: Euler's formula by computer
mathprize-2023-18.body:
Compute all intersection points exactly: strands $(i,k)$ (column $i$, $k^{\text{th}}$ unit of height) and $(j,l)$ with $i\ne j$ meet at $t=\frac{(k-l)-(i^2-j^2)}{2(i-j)}$ if the resulting point is inside the square. Collect distinct interior points $V_{\text{int}}$, the boundary vertices, and the edges (each strand is cut into one more piece than its number of interior points; the boundary is a cycle). Euler's formula for the bounded faces, $F=E-V+1$, gives $2,6,14,28,48,78$ for $n=1,\dots,6$.

**Answer: 78**

mathprize-2023-19.title: Lifting the exponent
mathprize-2023-19.body:
$4\equiv-1\pmod5$, so $4^k-1\equiv(-1)^k-1$, which is divisible by $5$ only for even $k$. For even $k=2j$, $4^k-1=16^j-1$ and $5\mid16-1$, so by the lifting-the-exponent lemma
$$v_5(16^j-1)=v_5(16-1)+v_5(j)=1+v_5(j)=v_5(5k)\ \ (\text{since }v_5(k)=v_5(j)).$$
(The official solution proves this via the binomial expansion of $(5-1)^k$ and Kummer's theorem.)

So
$$v_5(N)=\sum_{j=1}^{500}\left(1+v_5(j)\right)=500+\left(\left\lfloor\tfrac{500}{5}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\tfrac{500}{25}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\tfrac{500}{125}\right\rfloor\right)=500+100+20+4=624.$$

**Answer: 624**

mathprize-2023-19.title: Direct computation
mathprize-2023-19.body:
A short program that divides each $4^k-1$ ($k\le1000$, exact big integers) by $5$ as long as possible and adds up the counts returns $624$. This matches the formula: each even $k$ contributes $1+v_5(k)$, so the total is $\frac{1000}{2}+\frac{1000}{10}+\frac{1000}{50}+\frac{1000}{250}=500+100+20+4$.

**Answer: 624**

mathprize-2023-20.title: Humps and troughs
mathprize-2023-20.body:
Call a piece of graph that rises strictly from $0$ to $2\pi$ and falls back to $0$ a *hump*, and its negative (down to $-2\pi$ and back) a *trough*.

**Claim:** between consecutive zeros, $f_n$ is a hump or a trough. True for $n=1$. If $f_N$ is a hump on $[z_k,z_{k+1}]$, then as $f_N$ goes $0\to2\pi\to0$, $f_{N+1}=2\pi\sin f_N$ goes: hump (while $f_N$ runs over $[0,\pi]$), trough ($f_N\in[\pi,2\pi]$), trough (coming back), hump — i.e. hump, trough, trough, hump. A trough of $f_N$ similarly gives trough, hump, hump, trough.

The intervals we want are exactly where a trough is immediately followed by a hump (from the minimum $-2\pi$ to the next maximum $2\pi$). Let $B_n$ be the number of humps/troughs and $I_n$ the number of trough-then-hump pairs. Then $B_{n+1}=4B_n$, $B_1=2$, so $B_n=2\cdot4^{n-1}$. Each trough-hump boundary of $f_n$ remains one in $f_{n+1}$ (a trough ends with a trough and a hump starts with a hump), and each hump or trough creates exactly one new trough-hump pair inside it. So $I_{n+1}=I_n+B_n$ with $I_1=0$:
$$I_6=2(1+4+4^2+4^3+4^4)=2\cdot341=682.$$

**Answer: 682**

mathprize-2023-20.title: Check small cases numerically
mathprize-2023-20.body:
The recursion gives $I_n=\frac{4^n-4}{6}$: $I_2=2$, $I_3=10$, $I_4=42$. Sampling $f_n$ on a fine grid of $[0,2\pi]$ and counting consecutive extrema going from $-2\pi$ directly to $2\pi$ gives $2,10,42$ for $n=2,3,4$, confirming the pattern, so $I_6=\frac{4096-4}{6}=682$.

**Answer: 682**
